result:
There's a particular pleasure in noticing things that have no practical use whatsoever — the way a word sounds wrong the moment you stare at it too long, or how a familiar street looks foreign if you walk it backward. I want to spend some time on things like that, the small odd corners of thought that don't lead anywhere in particular but are worth visiting anyway.

Take maps. Not the GPS kind, which are really just instructions wearing a disguise, but the old kind, the ones drawn by people who hadn't seen most of what they were drawing. Medieval mapmakers filled the unknown edges of the world with sea monsters and the phrase "here be dragons," which sounds like superstition until you realize it's actually a remarkably honest cartographic convention. They were marking the boundary of knowledge itself. Everything inside the line was claimed, measured, named. Everything outside it was admitted ignorance, dressed up as a monster because a blank space looks like an oversight and a monster looks like a decision. I find something moving in that. We don't really do this anymore — our maps now cover the whole globe, satellite-stitched and seamless, and there's no "here be dragons" left anywhere on Earth. The dragons have all been relocated to other registers: the unmapped territories now are things like the inside of black holes, the first microsecond of the universe, or, more mundanely, what's happening inside another person's head when they go quiet in the middle of a conversation. We always need some edge of the map to put our monsters on.

I think about zero a lot, too, in an idle way — not the number itself but the fact that it had to be invented. It seems like it should be obvious, the most basic possible idea, nothing, but it took human civilizations thousands of years of mathematics to actually formalize it as a number you could compute with rather than just an absence you stepped around. The Romans had a numeral system that worked reasonably well for trade and engineering and never needed zero, because why would you write down a symbol for "I have none of this"? You'd just not mention it. Zero only becomes necessary once you need a placeholder — once you're doing positional arithmetic and need to distinguish 41 from 401 from 4001. It's a symbol invented to mark absence as a present thing, to give nothing a chair at the table. The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta gets a lot of credit for working out its arithmetic rules in the 7th century, including the genuinely difficult question of what happens when you divide by it, which he got wrong, understandably, since the honest answer is that the operation breaks math's furniture. We still don't have a satisfying answer; we just declare the operation undefined and move on, the mathematical equivalent of declining to discuss it further.

What strikes me about zero is how it demonstrates that even the most fundamental-seeming concepts are technologies. They were built, by particular people, at particular times, often slowly and through error, and once built they become invisible, baked so deep into how we think that we forget anyone had to invent them. Same with the number system generally, with the alphabet, with the very idea of a written word standing in for a spoken sound. Writing was invented maybe five or six separate times in human history, independently, by Sumerians and Egyptians and Chinese scribes and Mesoamerican societies, and every time it happened it followed a similar pattern: it started as accounting. Not poetry, not prayer, not love letters — inventories. Sumerian cuneiform's earliest tablets are receipts. So-and-so owes so-and-so this many sheep. The Iliad and the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Book of Job, all the foundational literature we think of as the wellspring of written culture, came later, riding on technology invented to track livestock. There's something almost comic about it, that the most transcendent uses of language were built on the chassis of bookkeeping. Maybe that's not even a coincidence — maybe you need a society organized enough to need careful accounting before you have a society organized enough to support people whose job is just to tell stories.

I keep circling back to the idea that big things are built out of small, unglamorous parts, and that the glamour comes later, applied retroactively. This seems true of almost everything. Cathedrals are stone and mortar and the unbelievably tedious labor of thousands of anonymous people hauling material up scaffolding for years; the transcendence you feel standing inside one, looking up into a ceiling that seems to defy the weight it's carrying, is real, but it's built entirely out of unglamorous physical labor and unglamorous physical engineering, none of which announces itself. The math is invisible. The labor is invisible. Only the result presents itself, and it presents itself as if it had arrived by some other means entirely, as if awe were a raw material rather than a byproduct.

Language does something similar with metaphor — we build abstract thought almost entirely out of physical metaphor and then forget we did it. We say we "grasp" an idea, that an argument doesn't "hold up," that someone is "warm" or "cold," that time is something you "spend" or "waste" or "save," as if it were money, or that you can be "in" a good mood as if a mood were a room. Cognitive linguists have spent a lot of effort cataloguing this, showing how thoroughly even our most rigorous thinking is scaffolded by bodily experience translated sideways into the abstract. We don't have direct, unmediated access to ideas like justice or time or love; we access them by way of metaphors borrowed from things we can touch and feel and move through. It means the boundary between "concrete" and "abstract" thought is thinner and more porous than it looks, and that a huge amount of philosophy is, underneath its vocabulary, an argument about which metaphor to use. Is time a river or a thief? Is the mind a container or a machine? You can have a real disagreement that looks like it's about deep truths but is actually about which image got chosen at the start, because the image quietly dictates what conclusions feel natural to draw from it.

There are words that don't translate, and I like collecting these the way some people collect coins, not because they reveal some mystical truth about a culture's soul (a claim I think gets overstated — most untranslatable words are untranslatable for fairly mundane reasons, like a language having merged two concepts English keeps separate) but because each one is a small reminder that the conceptual map your native language drew for you isn't the only possible map. German's "Vorfreude," the specific pleasure of anticipating something good, distinct from the pleasure of the thing itself. The Portuguese "saudade," a kind of longing for something absent that carries affection rather than just grief in it. Japanese has "mono no aware," the wistfulness of impermanence, the tenderness you feel toward something precisely because it won't last. English doesn't lack the feelings; it just never bothered to give them their own word, because no one was using them often enough, in a fixed enough form, to justify the shortcut. Vocabulary, in this sense, is mostly a record of what a community of speakers needed to say efficiently and often, not a record of what they were capable of feeling. The lack of a word for something is not a lack of the experience. It's just a lack of a shortcut for it, which means you have to build the meaning out of a sentence instead of grabbing it off a shelf, slower but not impossible.

This is maybe why I find translation, as an activity, kind of moving to think about, even though I encounter it constantly and rarely think about the mechanics. Every translated sentence is an admission that perfect equivalence is impossible and an attempt to do something almost as good anyway, with full knowledge of its own approximation. A good translator isn't trying to produce a sentence that means the same thing as the original; that's frequently not even achievable, especially with poetry, where sound and rhythm carry half the meaning and simply do not exist in another language's sound and rhythm. A good translator is trying to produce a sentence that does something equivalent to what the original sentence did to its original readers, which is a much stranger and more creative task than "say the same thing in different words." It's closer to writing a new poem under tight constraints than copying an old one.

I think about time differently depending on what I'm doing, which is itself a strange thing to notice. There's the time of being absorbed in something — working through a problem, reading a good book, having a conversation that actually goes somewhere — and that time has almost no texture to it at all; it passes and you don't feel the passing, you just look up afterward and find the light has changed. And then there's the time of waiting, which has unbelievable texture, every second separately wrapped, like waiting for results of something that matters, or sitting in a chair before a procedure, or the specific torment of watching a slow webpage load when you're checking something urgent. The actual clock doesn't care about this difference, ticks along uniformly regardless, but experienced time is wildly elastic, stretched and compressed depending on attention, and I don't think we've ever fully reconciled the clock's account of time with the felt account, even though we live by the clock's account almost exclusively now. Before mechanical clocks, time was task-based for most people — you did the milking, and then you did the next thing, and "an hour" wasn't a unit most people needed or used; the day organized itself around what needed doing, not around an external uniform grid laid over everything. The clock changed that relationship pretty completely, turned time into something you could be early or late for independent of any task, something with its own existence apart from what filled it. That's a strange kind of invention too, like zero: a way of marking and dividing something that has no natural divisions, imposing a grid on a thing that doesn't actually come pre-gridded.

I notice I keep returning to this same shape of observation — that some basic feature of how we think or live turns out, on inspection, to be a constructed thing rather than a natural one, a tool someone built rather than a fact of the universe. Money is like this. Borders are like this. The seven-day week is like this (the Babylonians get credit, tied loosely to the visible planetary bodies, and it's survived for millennia mostly through cultural inertia and the convenience of having settled on something rather than the particular virtue of seven). Even something as basic as the categories we sort emotions into — happy, sad, angry, afraid — turn out to vary across cultures and history in ways that suggest the categories themselves aren't simply discovered in the structure of human feeling but are partly built by the language used to talk about feeling, reinforcing certain boundaries and blurring others. None of this means these things are arbitrary or that we should discard them — money is a constructed fiction and also one of the more useful fictions humanity has ever maintained, clocks are an imposed grid and also indispensable for coordinating eight billion people's overlapping lives — but there's something clarifying about remembering the constructedness anyway. It keeps you from mistaking the map for the territory, to use yet another metaphor that's snuck into ordinary language so thoroughly we forget it's a metaphor at all, borrowed originally from a specific philosophical point about representation and now just sitting in everyday speech doing quiet work.

Maybe that's the throughline in all of this, if there has to be one: most of what feels given turns out to be made, and most of what feels made eventually starts to feel given, because that's what time does to human inventions — it sands the fingerprints off them. The alphabet feels given. Zero feels given. The week feels given. Clock time feels given. They are all, on inspection, things someone had to think up, defend, refine, and propagate, often against resistance, often slowly, often by accident as much as design. I don't think this is a depressing realization. If anything it suggests something almost the opposite of disenchantment — that the world we live in, including the parts of it that feel most solid and inevitable, is shot through with human decision, all the way down, in ways that are mostly invisible only because they worked well enough to disappear. The dragons on the edge of the old maps weren't really about ignorance. They were a kind of honesty, an admission built right into the document, that the map is always smaller than the world, that someone made it, and that there's always more past the edge than anyone's gotten around to drawing yet.
